problem: Addition: source says authority of the Government; candidate says 'the executive', a claim the source does not make. Also 'answers to' blurs 'is subordinate to'.
replacement: The absence of a central government will not, then, prove the destruction of the republics of the New World, as has often been claimed. Far from supposing that the American governments are not centralized enough, I shall show later that they are too centralized. The legislative bodies encroach on the authority of the government every day, and their tendency, like that of the French Convention, is to take it entirely for themselves. In these circumstances the social power is constantly changing hands, because it is subordinate to the power of the people, which in its awareness of its own strength is all too ready to forget the maxims of wisdom and foresight. Here lies its danger. Its vigor, and not its weakness, will probably be the cause of its eventual destruction.

problem: Nuance shift: source says the want of regulations is severely felt (in America) and frequently observed by Europeans; candidate makes Europeans the ones who feel it.
replacement: The system of local administration produces several different effects in America. The Americans seem to me to have gone beyond the limits of sound policy in isolating the administration of the government, for order, even in secondary matters, is of national importance. *r Because the State has no administrative officials of its own, stationed at various points across its territory, to whom it can give a common direction, it rarely tries to issue any general police regulations. The lack of these regulations is keenly felt, and Europeans frequently notice it. The appearance of disorder on the surface leads a European at first to imagine that society is in a state of anarchy, and he does not see his mistake until he has looked deeper into the subject. Certain undertakings matter to the whole State, but they cannot be carried out, because there is no national administration to direct them. Left to the efforts of the towns or counties, under the care of elected or temporary agents, they lead to no result, or at least to no lasting benefit.

It cannot be denied that the United States not infrequently feels the lack of those uniform regulations that govern the conduct of every inhabitant of France. Gross cases of social indifference and neglect are to be found, and from time to time disgraceful blemishes appear in complete contrast with the civilization around them. Useful undertakings that cannot succeed without constant attention and rigorous exactness are very often abandoned in the end, for in America, as in other countries, the people is subject to sudden impulses and short bursts of effort. The European is accustomed to finding an official always at hand to interfere in everything he undertakes, and he has some difficulty getting used to the complex machinery of township administration. In general it may be said that the lesser details of police, which make life easy and comfortable, are neglected in America, but that the essential guarantees of man in society are as strong there as anywhere else. In America the power that conducts the government is far less regular, less enlightened, and less learned than in Europe, but a hundred times more authoritative. In no country in the world do the citizens make such efforts for the common good. I know of no people that has established schools as numerous and as effective, places of public worship better suited to the needs of the inhabitants, or roads kept in better repair. Uniformity and permanence of design, the minute arrangement of details, *t and the perfection of an ingenious administration must not be looked for in the United States. But it is easy to find there the signs of a power that, if somewhat barbarous, is at least robust, and of a life that is full of accidents, but also cheered by animation and effort.

problem: 'adroitly handled' rendered 'skillfully exploited' adds a charge not in the source.
replacement: On the other hand, I am convinced that democratic nations are the most exposed to falling under the yoke of a central administration, for several reasons, among them the following. The constant tendency of these nations is to concentrate all the strength of the government in the hands of the only power that directly represents the people, because beyond the people nothing can be seen but a mass of equal individuals merged together. But when that same power already holds all the attributes of government, it can hardly refrain from reaching into the details of administration, and an opportunity to do so is sure to present itself in the end, as happened in France. In the French Revolution there were two impulses in opposite directions, which must never be confused. One favored liberty, the other despotism. Under the ancient monarchy the King was the sole author of the laws, and beneath the sovereign’s power certain half-destroyed vestiges of provincial institutions could still be made out. These provincial institutions were incoherent, loosely constructed, and often absurd. In the hands of the aristocracy they had sometimes been turned into instruments of oppression. The Revolution declared itself the enemy of royalty and of provincial institutions at the same time. It lumped together everything that had come before it, despotic power and the checks on its abuses alike, in indiscriminate hatred, and its tendency was both to overthrow and to centralize. This double character of the French Revolution is a fact that the friends of absolute power have skillfully handled. Can they be accused of working for despotism when they defend that central administration, which was one of the great innovations of the Revolution? *v In this way popularity may be won along with hostility to the rights of the people, and the secret slave of tyranny may be the professed admirer of freedom.
